title: What If You Could See Infrared?

sources.title: NASA Solar System Exploration (archived): Infrared Waves
Gracheva et al. (2010), Molecular basis of infrared detection by snakes, Nature
UC Santa Barbara / University of California: Mosquitoes sense infrared from body heat to help track humans down
Palczewska et al. (2014), Human infrared vision is triggered by two-photon chromophore isomerization, PNAS

scenes.narration: What if your eyes could see heat? Every person around you would glow, even in total darkness.
Tap like, then see what you'd notice first.
Your body shines brightest at about ten microns, more than ten times the wavelength of the reddest light your eyes catch now.
You already feel this light every day. The warmth from a campfire or a sun-baked sidewalk reaches your skin as infrared.
Some animals already do this. Pit vipers, pythons and boas sense infrared through pit organs, using a heat-sensitive protein related to the one behind the sting of wasabi.
And in 2024, scientists found mosquitoes use the infrared from our skin to help find us, from up to about seventy centimeters away.
You can even catch a sliver yourself. In lab tests, people saw pulses of near-infrared laser light, when two photons struck the eye together.
So in the dark, you'd stop seeing faces. You'd see warm shapes, a thermal image, the way a rattlesnake sees its next meal.

claims.claim: Humans at normal body temperature radiate most strongly in the infrared at about 10 microns
Warm objects such as people emit infrared regardless of visible light
Visible light ends around 700 nm (0.7 microns) at the red end

Pit-bearing snakes (vipers, pythons and boas) detect infrared via the pit organ using TRPA1, the most heat-sensitive vertebrate ion channel identified; they form a thermal image of prey; TRPA1 is the snake orthologue of the 'wasabi receptor'
Aedes aegypti mosquitoes use thermal infrared from skin-temperature sources, together with other cues, to find hosts at up to about 70 cm (2024 Nature study)
People perceived pulsed near-infrared laser light (~1000 nm) via two-photon isomerization of visual pigment
Humans feel infrared as heat, e.g. from a fire or a warm sidewalk

meta.title: What If You Could See Infrared?
meta.summary: Your body glows brightest in infrared, at about ten microns. Snakes and mosquitoes already use that glow, and in the lab, people have glimpsed a sliver of infrared too.
